[Meat ants](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Meat_Ant_(Iridomyrmex_purpureus)_(32733937383).jpg) (*Iridomyrmex purpureus*).

::: {.column width="70%"}

- In [Unit C](un_C.html) and [Unit D](un_D.html) we saw that binomial and Poisson regression may suffer from [overdispersion]{.orange}: the data are more variable than the model allows.

- This unit presents [quasi-likelihoods]{.blue} [@Wedderburn1974], a simple way to handle overdispersion [without]{.orange} specifying a distribution for $Y_i$: we only specify its [mean]{.blue} and its [variance]{.orange}.

- The unit has three parts: a [motivating example]{.blue}, the [theory]{.orange} of quasi-likelihoods, and the [complete analysis]{.grey} of the example.

- An alternative, [not covered]{.grey} in this course, is to replace the Poisson or the binomial with a different parametric distribution, e.g. the negative binomial.
:::

:::

:::callout-tip
The content of this Unit is covered in [Chapter 6]{.orange} of @Salvan2020. Alternatively, see [Sections 8.1 and 8.3]{.blue} of @Agresti2015.
:::

```{r}
#| include: false
# Data preparation and all the fitted models used in this unit
data(Ants)
Ants$Bread <- as.factor(Ants$Bread)
Ants$Filling <- as.factor(Ants$Filling)
Ants$Butter <- as.factor(Ants$Butter)

pv <- function(p) ifelse(p < 0.001, "<0.001", sprintf("%.3f", p))

# Poisson model
m_pois <- glm(Ant_count ~ Bread + Filling * Butter, family = poisson, data = Ants)
cf_pois <- summary(m_pois)$coefficients
X2 <- sum(residuals(m_pois, type = "pearson")^2)
X2_pvalue <- pchisq(X2, df = m_pois$df.residual, lower.tail = FALSE)

# Quasi-Poisson model
m_quasi <- glm(Ant_count ~ Bread + Filling * Butter,
  family = quasi(link = "log", variance = "mu"), data = Ants
)
cf_quasi <- summary(m_quasi)$coefficients
phi_hat <- summary(m_quasi)$dispersion

# Model simplification
d1 <- drop1(m_quasi, test = "Chisq")
m_quasi1 <- update(m_quasi, . ~ . - Bread)
d2 <- drop1(m_quasi1, test = "Chisq")

# Final model
m_final <- update(m_quasi1, . ~ . - Filling:Butter)
cf_final <- summary(m_final)$coefficients
phi_final <- summary(m_final)$dispersion
rel_change <- round(100 * (exp(coef(m_final)) - 1))

# Confidence and prediction intervals
newdata <- data.frame(Filling = "3", Butter = "1")
pred <- predict(m_final, newdata = newdata, type = "link", se.fit = TRUE)
mu_new <- exp(pred$fit)
ci_mean <- exp(pred$fit + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(0.975) * pred$se.fit)
pi_quasi <- qnorm(c(0.025, 0.975), mean = mu_new, sd = sqrt(phi_final * mu_new))
pi_pois <- qpois(c(0.025, 0.975), lambda = mu_new)

# Simulated data without overdispersion
set.seed(123)
x_sim <- rbinom(2000, size = 1, prob = 0.5)
y_sim <- rpois(2000, lambda = exp(1 + 3 * x_sim))
m_sim <- glm(y_sim ~ x_sim, family = poisson)
phi_sim <- sum(residuals(m_sim, type = "pearson")^2) / m_sim$df.residual
```

## The `Ants` data

- The `Ants` dataset of the `MLGdata` library comes from an experiment run by students of an Australian university [@Salvan2020]. The aim is to study which sandwiches [meat ants]{.orange} prefer.

- The [explanatory variables]{.blue} are three experimental factors:

  - `Bread` ($4$ types): rye, wholemeal, multigrain, white;
  - `Filling` ($3$ types): Vegemite, peanut butter, ham and pickles;
  - `Butter` ($2$ levels): present ($1$) or absent ($-1$).

- For each of the $4 \times 3 \times 2 = 24$ combinations, [two]{.orange} pieces of sandwich were placed near the entrance of an ant nest, for a total of $n = 48$ observations.

- The [response]{.blue} `Ant_count` is the number of ants on the sandwich after $5$ minutes.

## Exploratory analysis

```{r}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-align: center
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
boxplot(Ant_count ~ Bread, data = Ants, col = "grey85")
boxplot(Ant_count ~ Filling, data = Ants, col = "grey85")
boxplot(Ant_count ~ Butter, data = Ants, col = "grey85")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

- `Filling` and `Butter` seem to matter, whereas `Bread` has a weaker effect.

- The response is a [count]{.blue}, therefore a natural starting point is a [Poisson regression]{.orange} model with logarithmic link, including the `Filling`-`Butter` interaction ($p = 9$).

## A Poisson regression model

::: {.small-table}

```{r}
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Estimate = cf_pois[, 1], `Std. Error` = cf_pois[, 2], `p-value` = pv(cf_pois[, 4]),
    check.names = FALSE
  ),
  digits = 3, align = "r"
)
```

:::

- According to the Wald tests, `Bread2`, `Filling3` and both [interaction]{.orange} terms are significant at the $5\%$ level. 

- But can we trust these standard errors and the associated tests?

## Is there overdispersion?

- Relative to the Poisson model, [overdispersion]{.orange} means that $\text{var}(Y_i) = \phi\,\mu_i$ with $\phi > 1$. Hence, we need an [estimate]{.blue} of $\phi$.

- Recall from [Unit B](un_B.html) the [moment estimator]{.blue} of $\phi$ which, in the Poisson case, is
$$
\hat{\phi} = \frac{X^2}{n - p}, \qquad X^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{(y_i - \hat{\mu}_i)^2}{\hat{\mu}_i}.
$$
If the Poisson model is correct, we should find $\hat{\phi} \approx 1$.

- In the `Ants` data we obtain $X^2 =$ `r round(X2, 2)` on $n - p = 39$ degrees of freedom, hence $\hat{\phi} =$ `r round(X2 / m_pois$df.residual, 2)` (p-value of the $X^2$ test `r pv(X2_pvalue)`). 

- The variance is about [four times]{.orange} the Poisson one, so the Poisson standard errors are [too small]{.orange}.

:::callout-warning
A large $X^2$ may also be due to a [misspecified mean]{.blue}, e.g. omitted covariates or interactions, or a wrong link. 
:::

## A word of caution

- A tempting shortcut is to compare the sample mean and variance of the response. In the `Ants` data they are `r round(mean(Ants$Ant_count), 1)` and `r round(var(Ants$Ant_count))`. Is this enough to conclude that there is overdispersion? [No]{.orange}.

- The relation $\text{var}(Y_i) = \phi\,\mu_i$ concerns $Y_i$ [given the covariates]{.blue}, since $\mu_i$ depends on $\bm{x}_i$. 

- Consider $n = 2000$ observations from
$$
Y_i \overset{\text{ind}}{\sim} \text{Poisson}(\mu_i), \qquad \log{\mu_i} = 1 + 3 x_i, \qquad x_i \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \text{Bernoulli}(0.5),
$$
which have [no overdispersion]{.orange} by construction.

- The simulated data have mean `r round(mean(y_sim), 1)` and variance `r round(var(y_sim), 1)`, simply because the covariate shifts the mean. 

- Once the covariate is accounted for, the Poisson fit gives $X^2/(n-p) =$ `r round(phi_sim, 3)`.

## Quasi-likelihood assumptions

:::callout-note
The [quasi-likelihood]{.blue} approach only relies on the following [second-order]{.orange} assumptions:

- **(E.1)** $\quad\mathbb{E}(Y_i) = \mu_i = g^{-1}(\bm{x}_i^T\beta)$;

- **(E.2)** $\quad\text{var}(Y_i) = \dfrac{\phi}{\omega_i}v(\mu_i)$, with $\phi > 0$ [unknown]{.orange};

- **(E.3)** $\quad Y_i$ and $Y_j$ are independent for $i \neq j$.
:::

- These assumptions define a [semiparametric]{.blue} model: only the first two moments of $Y_i$ are specified, the distribution is not.

- A GLM with $Y_i \overset{\text{ind}}{\sim} \text{ED}(\mu_i, a_i(\phi)v(\mu_i))$ and $a_i(\phi) = \phi/\omega_i$ satisfies **(E.1)**-**(E.3)**, but it also specifies the [whole distribution]{.orange} of $Y_i$.

## On the choice of the variance function

- With identity link and $v(\mu_i) = \omega_i = 1$, **(E.1)**-**(E.3)** are essentially the [Gauss-Markov]{.grey} assumptions of [Unit A](un_A.html), with $\phi = \sigma^2$. The novelty concerns [counts]{.blue} and [proportions]{.blue}, where GLMs fix $\phi = 1$.

- Keeping the variance function of a GLM, **(E.2)** [inflates]{.orange} its variance by $\phi$: [overdispersion]{.orange} if $\phi > 1$, [underdispersion]{.blue} (rare) if $\phi < 1$.

- The two most common quasi-likelihood models are:
  - the [quasi-Poisson]{.blue} model, with $\text{var}(Y_i) = \phi\,\mu_i$;
  - the [quasi-binomial]{.orange} model, with $\text{var}(Y_i) = \phi\,\mu_i(1-\mu_i)/m_i$.

:::callout-warning
As noted in [Unit C](un_C.html), the quasi-binomial model makes sense only for [grouped]{.orange} data. With binary data ($m_i = 1$) we necessarily have $\text{var}(Y_i) = \mu_i(1-\mu_i)$, hence $\phi = 1$.
:::

:::callout-tip
The variance function $v(\cdot)$ need not be the one of a GLM: e.g. $v(\mu) = \mu^2(1-\mu)^2$ for proportions [@Wedderburn1974] is not the variance function of any [exponential dispersion family]{.orange}.
:::


## The quasi-score

- Without a likelihood, how do we estimate $\beta$? 

- Recall from [Unit B](un_B.html) that the [likelihood equations]{.blue} of a GLM are $q_r(\beta) = 0$, for $r=1,\dots,p$, where
$$
q_r(\beta) = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{(y_i - \mu_i)}{\text{var}(Y_i)}\frac{\partial \mu_i}{\partial \beta_r} = \frac{1}{\phi}\sum_{i=1}^n \omega_i\frac{(y_i - \mu_i)}{v(\mu_i)}\frac{x_{ir}}{g'(\mu_i)}.
$$

- These equations depend on the distribution of $Y_i$ [only]{.orange} through $\mathbb{E}(Y_i)$ and $\text{var}(Y_i)$, that is, only through assumptions **(E.1)** and **(E.2)**.

- Hence, we define $\hat{\beta}$ as the solution of $q_r(\beta) = 0$, and we call $q_r(\beta)$ the [quasi-score]{.blue}. These equations do not depend on $\phi$ and are solved with the [IRLS]{.orange} algorithm. 

- If $v(\cdot)$ is the variance function of a GLM, as in the quasi-Poisson and quasi-binomial models, $\hat{\beta}$ is (also) the [maximum likelihood estimate]{.blue} of that GLM.

## Properties of the quasi-score

- Let us regard the quasi-score $q_r(\beta)$ as a random variable, i.e. with $Y_i$ in place of $y_i$.

- Under **(E.1)**-**(E.3)** alone, it satisfies the [Bartlett identities]{.orange} of a genuine score function, namely $\mathbb{E}\{q_r(\beta)\} = 0$ and
$$
\mathbb{E}\{q_r(\beta)q_s(\beta)\} = -\mathbb{E}\left\{\frac{\partial q_r(\beta)}{\partial \beta_s}\right\} = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{\text{var}(Y_i)}\frac{\partial \mu_i}{\partial \beta_r}\frac{\partial \mu_i}{\partial \beta_s} = [\bm{X}^T\bm{W}\bm{X}]_{rs},
$$
where $\bm{W} = \text{diag}(w_1,\dots,w_n)$ contains the weights of [Unit B](un_B.html), that is
$$
w_i = \frac{1}{\text{var}(Y_i)g'(\mu_i)^2} = \frac{1}{\phi}\frac{\omega_i}{v(\mu_i) g'(\mu_i)^2}.
$$

:::callout-tip
The quasi-score behaves like a genuine score, even though no distribution has been specified. This explains the name [quasi-likelihood]{.blue}, and it is the key to the asymptotic results.
:::

## Asymptotic properties of $\hat{\beta}$

:::callout-warning
Under the assumptions **(E.1)**-**(E.3)** and (mild) regularity conditions, the estimator $\hat{\beta}$ is [consistent]{.blue} and [asymptotically normal]{.orange}:
$$
\hat{\beta} \: \dot{\sim} \: \text{N}_p\left(\beta, (\bm{X}^T\bm{W}\bm{X})^{-1}\right).
$$
:::

- The result is [formally identical]{.orange} to the one of [Unit B](un_B.html), but it holds under much [weaker assumptions]{.blue}, as for the OLS estimator under the Gauss-Markov assumptions.

- Does it make sense to talk about the [exact]{.blue} distribution of $\hat{\beta}$? [No]{.orange}: it would require the distribution of $Y_i$, which we deliberately left unspecified.

- Consistency only requires **(E.1)**: if the [mean]{.blue} is correctly specified, $\hat{\beta}$ is consistent even when $v(\mu_i)$ is wrong. The [standard errors]{.orange}, however, rely on **(E.2)**.

## A recipe for overdispersion using quasi-likelihoods

- The dispersion $\phi$ is estimated with the [method of moments]{.blue} estimator already used for the `Ants` data, which is [consistent]{.orange} under **(E.1)**-**(E.3)**. In general:
$$
\hat{\phi} = \frac{X^2}{n - p} = \frac{1}{n - p}\sum_{i=1}^n \omega_i \frac{(y_i - \hat{\mu}_i)^2}{v(\hat{\mu}_i)}.
$$

- The standard errors are obtained from $(\bm{X}^T\hat{\bm{W}}\bm{X})^{-1}$, plugging in $\hat{\beta}$ and $\hat{\phi}$. The weights $w_i$ are [inversely proportional]{.orange} to $\phi$.

:::callout-note
#### Variance inflation in a nutshell

When $v(\cdot)$ is the variance function of a GLM, as in the quasi-Poisson and quasi-binomial models:

1. Fit the [ordinary GLM]{.blue} and keep its maximum likelihood estimate $\hat{\beta}$.

2. Multiply the [standard errors]{.orange} of the GLM by $\sqrt{\hat{\phi}}$, that is $[\widehat{\text{se}}_\text{quasi}(\hat{\beta})]_j = \sqrt{\hat{\phi}}\,[\widehat{\text{se}}_\text{glm}(\hat{\beta})]_j$.
:::

## The quasi-log-likelihood

- To compare nested models we need something like a log-likelihood. Under **(E.1)**-**(E.3)** we define the [quasi-log-likelihood]{.blue}
$$
\ell_Q(\beta, \phi) = \sum_{i=1}^n \int_{y_i}^{\mu_i} \frac{\omega_i(y_i - t)}{\phi\,v(t)}\,\mathrm{d}t, \qquad \mu_i = g^{-1}(\bm{x}_i^T\beta),
$$
provided that these integrals exist.

- Its gradient is the [quasi-score]{.orange}, that is $\partial \ell_Q(\beta, \phi)/\partial \beta_r = q_r(\beta)$. Indeed, by the chain rule, the derivative of the $i$th integral is $\omega_i(y_i - \mu_i)/\{\phi\,v(\mu_i)\} \times \partial \mu_i / \partial \beta_r$.

- Since $\ell_Q(\beta, \phi)$ is a function of $\beta$, its second derivatives $\partial q_r(\beta)/\partial \beta_s$ are [symmetric]{.blue} in $r$ and $s$, as for a genuine log-likelihood.

- In general $\ell_Q(\beta, \phi)$ is [not]{.orange} a log-likelihood. However, in the Poisson case ($\omega_i = 1$, $v(t) = t$, $\phi = 1$) we get $\ell_Q(\beta, 1) = \sum_{i=1}^n(y_i \log{\mu_i} - \mu_i)$, up to constants, which is the [Poisson log-likelihood]{.blue}.

## Comparing nested models

- The quantity $D(\bm{y}; \bm{\mu}) = -2\phi\,\ell_Q(\beta, \phi)$ is called [quasi-deviance]{.blue}. When $v(\cdot)$ is the variance function of a GLM, it coincides with the [deviance]{.orange} of [Unit B](un_B.html), e.g. the Poisson or the binomial one.

- Let $M_0 \subset M_1$ be two [nested models]{.grey}, with $p_0$ and $p$ parameters, and let $q = p - p_0$. The [quasi-log-likelihood ratio]{.blue} statistic is
$$
W = 2[\ell_Q(\hat{\beta}, \hat{\phi}) - \ell_Q(\hat{\beta}_0, \hat{\phi})] = \frac{D(\bm{y}; \hat{\bm{\mu}}_0) - D(\bm{y}; \hat{\bm{\mu}})}{\hat{\phi}} \: \dot{\sim} \: \chi^2_q,
$$
where $\hat{\phi}$ is estimated from the [larger]{.orange} model.

:::callout-warning
- The (quasi-)deviances must [not]{.orange} be used as goodness-of-fit statistics, since $\phi$ is unknown.

- There is no likelihood, therefore the [AIC]{.orange} is [not available]{.orange}.
:::

## The quasi-Poisson model

- With the same mean structure, we obtain $\hat{\phi} =$ `r round(phi_hat, 2)`: the standard errors are multiplied by $\sqrt{\hat{\phi}} =$ `r round(sqrt(phi_hat), 2)`.

::: {.small-table}

```{r}
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Estimate = cf_quasi[, 1],
    `SE (Poisson)` = cf_pois[, 2], `SE (quasi)` = cf_quasi[, 2],
    `p-value (Poisson)` = pv(cf_pois[, 4]), `p-value (quasi)` = pv(cf_quasi[, 4]),
    check.names = FALSE
  ),
  digits = 3, align = "r"
)
```

:::

- The [estimates]{.blue} are identical, but the standard errors are larger: the tests are affected.

## Model simplification

- The larger standard errors suggest a [simpler]{.blue} model. We remove one term at a time, using the quasi-log-likelihood ratio statistic $W$ and its $\chi^2_q$ approximation.

```{r}
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Model = c("Full model", "Full model", "Without Bread"),
    `Removed term` = c("Bread", "Filling:Butter", "Filling:Butter"),
    q = c(d1["Bread", "Df"], d1["Filling:Butter", "Df"], d2["Filling:Butter", "Df"]),
    W = c(d1["Bread", "scaled dev."], d1["Filling:Butter", "scaled dev."], d2["Filling:Butter", "scaled dev."]),
    `p-value` = pv(c(d1["Bread", "Pr(>Chi)"], d1["Filling:Butter", "Pr(>Chi)"], d2["Filling:Butter", "Pr(>Chi)"])),
    check.names = FALSE
  ),
  digits = 3, align = "llrrr"
)
```

- Neither `Bread` nor the `Filling`-`Butter` interaction is relevant, once overdispersion is accounted for.

- The final model only includes `Filling` and `Butter`, with $p = 4$ parameters.

## The final model

```{r}
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Estimate = cf_final[, 1], `Std. Error` = cf_final[, 2], `p-value` = pv(cf_final[, 4]),
    `exp(Estimate)` = exp(cf_final[, 1]),
    check.names = FALSE
  ),
  digits = 3, align = "r"
)
```

- Under the logarithmic link, $\exp(\beta_j)$ is the [multiplicative change]{.blue} of the mean number of ants ([Unit D](un_D.html)). The estimated dispersion is $\hat{\phi} =$ `r round(phi_final, 2)`.

- Compared to Vegemite, [ham and pickles]{.orange} attract on average about `r rel_change["Filling3"]`% more ants, and peanut butter about `r rel_change["Filling2"]`% more (borderline significant).

- The presence of [butter]{.blue} increases the mean number of ants by about `r rel_change["Butter1"]`%. The type of bread is irrelevant.

## References
